description: Team HOKKAIDO ANALOG FINDER, based in Sapporo. We are a 2-person team building a map-based tool that scores Hokkaido's volcanic and cold-region terrain as analog sites for Moon and Mars base testing and training, using NASA Earth observation data and published research criteria. Our skills cover systems engineering, programming, and design. Let's explore the next frontier from Hokkaido!
summary:
On Mars, there is no rescue helicopter. If an astronaut walks out from base, the only question that matters is: can they walk back before oxygen and cooling water run out?

WALKBACK is a Martian map that answers that question before the walk starts. For a route around Jezero Crater, it computes usable time (6.0 hours, limited by both oxygen and cooling water), the returnable area (66 km²), and whether each route is safe to walk, using real terrain, temperature, and EVA data. A planned 5:36-hour route is judged walkable — or flagged to turn back — before the astronaut leaves.

The same method is tested against Hokkaido's volcanic and cold terrain, showing how Earth analog sites can rehearse Mars walks on Earth. WALKBACK answers Challenge #11, Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map, by turning a map into a go / no-go decision for human survival.
details:
What it does: WALKBACK plans a walking route on Mars and judges whether the astronaut can return alive. It combines slope and footing from Jezero Crater elevation data, temperature-dependent cooling-water use from Perseverance MEDA weather measurements, oxygen budgeting with a 20% reserve, and a two-speed walking model (normal 3.6–4.5 km/h, emergency 6.28 km/h) grounded in EVA records (368 EVAs). The app shows the route, its elevation profile, remaining oxygen and water by departure time, and the area reachable within the usable time.

How it works: Terrain comes from HiRISE elevation grids via NASA's Solar System Trek; map tiles are Viking / MOLA and HiRISE ortho imagery. The route engine runs in Rust (compiled to WebAssembly) with a TypeScript front end; an in-browser Q&A assistant (Qwen3 via pi-rs, running locally in WebAssembly) answers questions about the current route. A supporting Earth-analogs view compares Moon and Mars candidate sites with Hokkaido terrain, so the same walk can be rehearsed on Earth.

Goal and next steps: The goal is a walk-back limit that a crew can trust before stepping out. Next steps are live weather ingestion, finer terrain sampling on steep sections, and field validation of the Hokkaido rehearsal routes.

References:

- Atwood-Stone, C. & McEwen, A. S. (2013) — slope limit of 30° for traversability

- EVA records dataset used in the app (368 parsed EVAs; 375 raw rows including 0:00-duration aborted entries)

- NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, Challenge #11: Interplanetary Survival Guide — Martian Map

- Tools: Rust / WebAssembly, TypeScript / React, pi-rs (Qwen3 in-browser), Remotion

Use of AI:

AI was used in two places, and both are disclosed here.

(1) In the product: the in-app question assistant runs Qwen3 in the browser (pi-rs, WebAssembly) on the user's device; it answers questions about the route currently on screen and performs no remote inference.

(2) In development: Claude, Gemini via Antigravity (Google Antigravity), Muse, and ChatGPT assisted with research, code review, debugging, literature search, and drafting the presentation slides and submission text; the team logo was generated with an AI image-generation tool. The 30-second demo video was assembled with Remotion from real screenshots of the working app — it contains no AI-generated imagery or video. All scientific numbers, data choices, and the final submission text were decided and verified by the team.
